# Setup: VS Code and Google Colab {.unnumbered}

All the notebooks and labs in this course run on **Google Colab**, Google's free service for running Python notebooks on its machines, some of which have a GPU. The **labs** are done in **VS Code** on your own laptop, with the notebook running on a Colab machine through Google's Colab extension: this is how notebooks are used in research, and the labs are where you get used to it. The **course notebooks** that go with each session page can also be opened directly in Colab in the browser. Either way, nothing has to be installed on your laptop apart from VS Code and git, and every student works in the same environment.

| What you need | Why |
|------------------------|------------------------|
| A **Google account** (a free one is enough) | Colab runs your code on Google's machines |
| **VS Code** on your laptop, with the extensions **Jupyter**, **Python** and **Google Colab** | To open, edit and run the lab notebooks |
| **git** | To get all the course notebooks in one go and keep them up to date, and to keep your own work under version control (Session 2) |

Every lab notebook has an **Open in VS Code** link (on the session page, in Canvas and in the lab quiz), and every course notebook an **Open in Colab** badge. All notebooks fetch their data from the course's GitHub repository, so they run the same way everywhere. Do Parts 1 and 2 before the first lab in Session 2, and check that a notebook runs, so that the lab time is spent on the lab.

## Part 1: Install VS Code, git and the extensions

1.  Install [VS Code](https://code.visualstudio.com/) and [git](https://git-scm.com/downloads) if you do not already have them.
2.  In VS Code, open the Extensions view (Ctrl+Shift+X, or Cmd+Shift+X on a Mac) and install **Python** and **Jupyter** (both by Microsoft) and **Google Colab** (by Google).
3.  Check that you can sign in to Google in a browser with the account you want to use for the course.

## Part 2: Get the course notebooks into VS Code (once)

1.  Click **[Clone the course notebooks into VS Code](vscode://vscode.git/clone?url=https%3A%2F%2Fgithub.com%2FElofssonLab%2Fkb8029-book.git)**. Your browser asks whether to open VS Code: allow it. (Or, in VS Code: Command Palette, Ctrl+Shift+P or Cmd+Shift+P → **Git: Clone** → `https://github.com/ElofssonLab/kb8029-book.git`.)
2.  Choose where to save the folder `kb8029-book` (about 100 MB), and open it when VS Code offers to. The notebooks are in its `notebooks` folder.
3.  Before each lab, get the latest version: Command Palette → **Git: Pull**. The teachers sometimes fix a lab shortly before it is used.

## Part 3: Run a lab notebook on Colab from VS Code {#open-in-vscode}

Google's **Colab** extension for VS Code (released November 2025) lets a notebook that is open in VS Code run on a Colab machine:

1.  Click the lab's **Open in VS Code** link. The first time, the page that opens asks for the full path of your `kb8029-book` folder (for example `C:\Users\you\kb8029-book` or `/Users/you/kb8029-book`) and remembers it; after that, its button opens the notebook straight in VS Code. You can also open it yourself: in VS Code press Ctrl+P (Cmd+P on a Mac) and type the notebook's name, for example `session04-lab.ipynb`.

2.  Click **Select Kernel** (top right) → **Colab** → **Auto Connect** (or choose a runtime with a GPU), and sign in with your Google account when asked.

3.  Run the first cells. Most notebooks start with an install cell, which installs the few packages that Colab does not already have (for example Biopython); this takes a few seconds each time you connect to a new machine.

4.  When you need a GPU (mainly Sessions 9-12), check that you got one:

    ``` python
    import torch
    print(torch.cuda.is_available(), torch.cuda.get_device_name(0) if torch.cuda.is_available() else "")
    ```

Your changes are saved in your own copy of the notebook in `kb8029-book`. If **Git: Pull** complains that a file you changed would be overwritten, keep your version under another name (for example `session04-lab-mine.ipynb`) and pull again.

Things to know:

- **The code runs on Google's machine.** It cannot see files on your laptop, even though the notebook file is open in VS Code. The course notebooks download what they need from the course's GitHub repository, so they work anyway. For your own files, upload them, or mount Google Drive (Command Palette → **Colab: Mount Google Drive to Server...**).
- **Colab machines are temporary.** Everything on them, including installed packages and files the notebook wrote, disappears when the session ends. Your notebook itself, with its code and output, is saved on your laptop by VS Code. Save other results you want to keep (download them, or write them to Drive).
- **The free GPU is limited.** A session is closed after a period of inactivity or when your quota is used up, and a GPU is not always available. Ask for a GPU only when the notebook needs one, and when you are done, release the machine with **Colab: Remove Server**.
- **No terminal tools.** Everything in the labs is done from Python: the sequence searches and alignments in Sessions 4 and 5 call EMBL-EBI's web services (HMMER, Clustal Omega, InterPro), and in Session 6 PyMOL runs inside the notebook and structure searches go to the Foldseek web service.

## Part 4: Course notebooks in the browser

The course notebooks that go with each session page have an **Open in Colab** badge. Click it, choose **Runtime → Change runtime type → T4 GPU** if the notebook needs a GPU, and run the cells. This works from any computer. **File → Save a copy in Drive** keeps your own copy with your changes; without it, your edits are lost when you close the tab. You can also open a course notebook from your `kb8029-book` folder in VS Code, exactly as a lab.

## Troubleshooting {#troubleshooting}

**The Open in VS Code button does nothing, or VS Code says the file does not exist.** Check the folder path on the page (it must be the `kb8029-book` folder itself), and that the clone in Part 2 worked. Opening the notebook by name with Ctrl+P always works.

**VS Code does not offer Colab under Select Kernel.** Check that the Google Colab extension is installed and enabled in a *local* VS Code window, and reload the window (Command Palette → **Developer: Reload Window**).

**`ModuleNotFoundError`.** The runtime is new and the install cell has not been run in it. Run the notebook from the top.

**`FileNotFoundError` for a file you can see on your laptop.** The code runs on Colab, not on your laptop: upload the file, or read it from Drive.

**No GPU, or `torch.cuda.is_available()` is `False`.** You were given a machine without a GPU, or the free GPU quota is used up for now. Choose a GPU runtime explicitly, try again later, or run the notebook on the CPU: the course notebooks are small enough for that, only slower.

**The connection drops in the middle of a long cell.** Colab closes idle and long-running free sessions. Reconnect, run the notebook from the top, and save intermediate results to Drive if a step takes long.

| **The course server**, `students.bioinfo.se`, through VS Code | A Linux machine with the course's conda environment, the command-line tools (BLAST, HMMER, MMseqs2, ...) and all course data; no GPU | Most labs and notebooks that need tools or large data |

## Part 1: An SSH key

SSH is a way to connect securely (using an encrypted connection) between your computer and another computer. In our case the server does not use passwords ,instead you will log in using an **SSH key pair**:

- a **private key** (for example `id_ed25519`), which stays on your computer and is never shared, not even with the teachers;
- a **public key** (the same name ending in `.pub`), which you send to the teachers. It is added to the server, and only someone holding the matching private key can then log in as you.

Most login problems last year came from Windows computers holding more than one set of keys, so that the key sent in was not the key VS Code used. The steps below avoid that by creating the key in one known place and telling VS Code explicitly which file to use.

### Mac and Linux

Open a terminal and run:

``` sh
ls ~/.ssh/                       # do you already have id_ed25519 and id_ed25519.pub?
ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "your-username"
```

If `id_ed25519` already exists, you can reuse it (skip `ssh-keygen`). Otherwise accept the default location and choose a passphrase (you can leave it empty, but a passphrase protects the key if your laptop is stolen). Your public key is now in `~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub`, to see it do:

``` sh
cat ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub
```

### Windows

Use **PowerShell**, and Windows' own OpenSSH, which comes with Windows 10 and 11 and is the SSH that VS Code uses by default. **IMPORTANT:** Do **not** create the key with PuTTY/PuTTYgen, Git Bash or WSL for this course: each of those can store keys somewhere else, or in another format, which is how the wrong key ends up being used.

1.  Open **PowerShell** (Start menu → type "PowerShell").

2.  Check which `ssh` you have, and what keys already exist:

    ``` powershell
    Get-Command ssh              # should be C:\Windows\System32\OpenSSH\ssh.exe
    ls $HOME\.ssh                # existing keys, if any
    ```

    If `Get-Command ssh` finds nothing, install the OpenSSH client: Settings → System → Optional features → Add a feature → "OpenSSH Client".

3.  Create the key:

    ``` powershell
    ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "your-username"
    ```

    Accept the default location. It saves the key pair as `C:\Users\<you>\.ssh\id_ed25519` and `C:\Users\<you>\.ssh\id_ed25519.pub`. If `ssh-keygen` asks whether to overwrite an existing key, answer **no** and reuse the existing one instead (overwriting breaks anything that key was used for).

4.  Show the public key:

    ``` powershell
    Get-Content $HOME\.ssh\id_ed25519.pub
    ```

### Send the public key

The public key is **one line** that starts with `ssh-ed25519` and ends with the comment you gave (your username). Send that line, and only that line, to the Arne Elofsson [mailto://arne\@bioinfo.se](mailto://arne@bioinfo.se){.uri} . Never send the file without `.pub`. Once you have sent the key and it has been added to the setup system you should be able to access the server without using a password.

## Part 2: Connect VS Code to the server

### The SSH configuration file

An entry in your SSH configuration file gives the server a short name and fixes which key is used. Open it from VS Code, so it ends up in the right place with the right name:

1.  Install the extension **Remote - SSH** (by Microsoft; Extensions view, Ctrl+Shift+X or Cmd+Shift+X).

2.  Command Palette (Ctrl+Shift+P or Cmd+Shift+P) → **Remote-SSH: Open SSH Configuration File...** → choose the file in your home folder (`~/.ssh/config` on Mac and Linux, `C:\Users\<you>\.ssh\config` on Windows).

3.  Add these lines, with your own username:

    ```         
    Host kb8029-server
        HostName students.bioinfo.se
        User your-username
        IdentityFile ~/.ssh/id_ed25519
        IdentitiesOnly yes
    ```

    On Windows, write the key's full path instead: `IdentityFile C:/Users/<you>/.ssh/id_ed25519` (forward slashes work). `IdentitiesOnly yes` makes SSH offer only that key, and nothing else it finds.

If you edit the file in Notepad instead, make sure it is saved as `config` with no extension (Notepad likes to add `.txt`).

### Test from a terminal first

Once the teachers confirm that your key has been added you can:

``` sh
ssh kb8029-server
```

The first time, SSH shows the server's fingerprint and asks whether to continue: answer `yes`. You should get a Linux prompt on `students.bioinfo.se`; type `exit` to leave. If it fails, see [Troubleshooting](#troubleshooting) below before trying VS Code, because VS Code only adds another layer on top.

### Connect from VS Code

1.  Command Palette → **Remote-SSH: Connect to Host...** → `kb8029-server`. (Or click the green `><` button in the bottom-left corner.)
2.  A new VS Code window opens. If asked, choose **Linux** as the server's platform. The first connection takes a minute while VS Code installs its helper on the server (in `~/.vscode-server`).
3.  The bottom-left corner now says **SSH: kb8029-server**. Everything in this window, the file explorer, the terminal and running code, happens on the server, not on your laptop.
4.  **File → Open Folder...** and open your home folder (for example `/home/your-username`), or a `kb8029` folder you create inside it.

### Python and notebooks on the server

Extensions for a remote window run on the server, so they are installed separately there:

1.  Extensions view → search **Python** and **Jupyter** (both by Microsoft) → **Install in SSH: kb8029-server**.

2.  Open a terminal in VS Code (Terminal → New Terminal) and activate the course environment:

    ``` sh
    conda activate kb8029            # [to be confirmed: environment name]
    python -c "import torch, Bio; print(torch.__version__)"
    ```

3.  Open or create a notebook (`.ipynb`), click **Select Kernel** (top right) → **Python Environments** → **kb8029**. For a plain `.py` file, the same choice is under **Python: Select Interpreter**.

To get the course notebooks onto the server, clone the book's repository into your home folder (this might be useful so you do not have to copy the notebooks):

``` sh
git clone https://github.com/ElofssonLab/kb8029-book.git
```

The course data are on the server in **`/data/kb8029/`**. Read them from there; don't copy large files into your home folder as the hard drive space on the machine is limited. For convenience we put all the notebooks there.


### The PDC cluster

A limited number of GPU machines (gpuX.bioinfo.se) will be made available during the course. These can be used. However, the GPU can (in general) only be used by one student at a time, and we only have a limited set of such machines, Therefore, they might not always be available.

## Troubleshooting the server connection {#troubleshooting-ssh}

**`Permission denied (publickey)`.** The server did not accept any key you offered. Either your key has not been added yet, or SSH offered a different key from the one you sent. Run the connection with verbose output and look for the lines `Offering public key:` and `Server accepts key:`:

``` sh
ssh -v kb8029-server
```

The file named after `Offering public key:` must be the private half of the public key you sent. If it isn't, fix `IdentityFile` in your configuration file. You can compare fingerprints: `ssh-keygen -lf ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub` prints the fingerprint of the key you sent.

**Windows: several SSH programs.** If you have Git for Windows, PuTTY or WSL, you may have keys in several places:

- **WSL** keeps its own `~/.ssh` inside Linux, invisible to Windows' SSH and to VS Code.
- **PuTTYgen** saves keys as `.ppk`, which OpenSSH cannot read. If that is your only key, open it in PuTTYgen and use **Conversions → Export OpenSSH key**, or simply make a new key as in Part 1.
- **Git Bash** can have a different home folder from PowerShell, and put its keys elsewhere.

VS Code uses Windows' OpenSSH (`C:\Windows\System32\OpenSSH\ssh.exe`) unless the setting **Remote.SSH: Path** says otherwise. Check that setting is empty, or points to that file.

**`UNPROTECTED PRIVATE KEY FILE` or `bad permissions`.** SSH refuses a private key that other users can read. On Mac and Linux you can change this using this command `chmod 600 ~/.ssh/id_ed25519`. On Windows this happens when the key file was copied from elsewhere; creating the key with `ssh-keygen` as in Part 1 avoids it.

**VS Code keeps reconnecting or hangs at "Setting up SSH host".** Check that `ssh kb8029-server` works in a terminal. Then Command Palette → **Remote-SSH: Kill VS Code Server on Host...** → `kb8029-server`, and connect again. **Remote-SSH: Show Log** shows what went wrong.

**`conda: command not found`.** Your shell on the server has not been set up for conda. Run `conda init` once , then open a new terminal.

- VS Code documentation, [Remote development using SSH](https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/remote/ssh) and [Remote development tips and tricks](https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/remote/troubleshooting) (including SSH keys on Windows)
- Microsoft, [Get started with OpenSSH for Windows](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-server/administration/openssh/openssh_install_firstuse)
:::
